comment: The village arc (canon section 7, arc 10): The Unsent Letters. Multiplayer and cumulative. Opens at the first dawn after the clock is mended (day 2+); one stray letter drifts into Fen's dead-letter drawer each dawn after (sequenced by the world counter letters-arrived, seven in all). Any dreamer carries a letter to the keeper it nearly means and hears how that keeper came to the village; each delivery while the arc is open counts toward the world counter letters-delivered. Endings: found-letters (the fifth delivery, by anyone, closes it; the Night of Found Letters follows at the next dusk), dead-letter (fourteen days pass first: Fen ties the rest with ribbon and shuts the drawer). Letters carried or arriving after the Night can still be delivered for their reveals.

things.name: dead-letter drawer
things.seed: a deep oak drawer under Fen's counter, lined with blue paper and left open a hand's width; Fen keeps the stray letters in it, the ones addressed nearly to somebody here, until someone carries them

state_text.locked: It is shut now and tied round with blue ribbon, and Fen has chalked on the front: ANOTHER WINTER.

do.text: The drawer is already open a hand's width, and that is as far as Fen likes it. You can see what waits inside from where you stand; anything in it is for the taking, if it is yours to take.

things.name: crayon letter
things.seed: a letter folded small and addressed in big wobbly crayon; where the stamp should go, someone has drawn a sun, crossed it out, and drawn a lantern instead
things.text: The front is addressed in big wobbly crayon: TO THE ONE WHO LIGHTS THE LAMP OUTSIDE MY WINDOW. A lantern is drawn where the stamp should be, and through the thin paper you can just make out two crayon words inside: I WAVE.

do.text: Bell is fast asleep, one arm flung over their eyes and the butter-yellow scarf wound twice round their chin. You tuck the letter away again. It can wait until the lamps want lighting.

Bell reads the crayon letter twice, and the soot on their cheek creases into a grin. 'I waved back, you know. Every window.' They fold it into the butter-yellow scarf. 'First dusk I ever came down here, Wend was lighting this square alone, slow as moss, and held out the pole and said the lanterns liked company. I never did give it back.'
{actor} carried a stray crayon letter to Bell, and Bell told how they first came to the village.

things.name: marble letter
things.seed: an envelope addressed in careful, pressed-hard pencil, with a glass marble rolling in one corner; it clicks softly whenever it is tipped
things.text: In careful, pressed-hard pencil: TO WHOEVER MENDS THINGS (PLEASE). A glass marble rolls in the corner of the envelope, as if it has been sent along to say sorry.

do.text: Tace tips the marble into their palm and holds it to the lamp, where it throws a small green light across the bench. 'I broke a clock once, when I was about as big as this handwriting. Carried the pieces up those stairs in my apron.' Their hands go still, then carry on. 'Wend didn't want paying. Wend handed me a loupe, and I never went back down.'
{actor} carried a stray letter with a marble in it to Tace, and Tace told how they came up to the loft as a child.

things.name: button letter
things.seed: an envelope with a brown coat button stitched to one corner in thick grey thread, so it would not blow away
things.text: A brown coat button is stitched to the corner with thick grey thread. In a round, patient hand: TO WHOEVER FINDS MY BUTTON. IT MATCHES THIS ONE.

do.text: Mott opens the tin, finds the brown button that has lived there for years, and holds it to the letter's corner: a match, thread and all. He tucks the letter in beside it. 'Don't remember coming here myself,' he says after a while. 'First thing I remember is this broom, and the floor.' His thumb settles over the small folded thing in the tin, and stays.
{actor} carried a stray letter with a button on it to Mott, and the button in Mott's tin matched it, thread and all.

things.name: string-tied letter
things.seed: a fat envelope tied up in kitchen string with a careful bow, labeled on the back the way a jar would be
things.text: Tied up in kitchen string, the envelope reads: TO THE ONE WHO KEEPS THINGS FOR LATER. On the back, as if it were a jar: OPEN WHEN THERE IS TIME.

do.text: Umber unties the string, reads, and writes a label for the envelope before she says a word: KEPT FOR LATER. ARRIVED. She shelves it among the jars. 'When I came, this cellar held three jars and one lantern, and Wend knew every hour in it by name.' She turns a jar a quarter-turn. 'Wend couldn't bear to throw a thing away. Nor can I, it seems.'
{actor} carried a stray string-tied letter to Umber, and Umber told what the cellar was like when she first came.

things.name: tea-stained letter
things.seed: a soft envelope with a pale ring on it where a teacup once stood, the pencil address smudged a little by a warm thumb
things.text: There is a pale ring on the envelope where a cup once stood. In quick soft pencil: TO WHOEVER WAITED UP FOR ME.

do.text: Linden presses the tea towel to her mouth before she has even finished reading. 'Oh, lamb,' she says. 'Oh, bless.' She props the letter behind the kettle, where it will keep warm. 'I came here waiting up for someone, long ago. Can't think who, now. I waited so long I got good at it, and the house sort of grew up round me.'

things.name: grass-stained letter
things.seed: a green-smudged envelope that smells of cut grass, with a clover pressed flat inside
things.text: The envelope is green-smudged and smells of cut grass. In a hand that seems to have walked while it wrote: TO THE ONE WHO WALKED ME HOME.

do.text: Sorrel holds the letter very still, the way they wait for an hour to land. 'Walked someone home once, I think,' they say at last. 'Came along the Dusk Road myself one evening, with nowhere in particular to be, and the sky was so kind I stayed to watch it.' They tuck the pressed clover into their hatband, beside the sorrel. 'Still watching.'
{actor} carried a stray grass-stained letter to Sorrel, and Sorrel told how they came along the Dusk Road and stayed.

things.name: seed-packet letter
things.seed: a letter written on the back of an old paper seed packet, its picture faded past reading; a few seeds still rattle in one corner
things.text: It is written on the back of an old seed packet, and a few seeds still rattle in one corner. In a slow, round hand: TO WHOEVER IS MINDING MY GARDEN.

do.text: Quill turns the seed packet front and back and goes pink to the ears. He tips the seeds into his palm as if they might wake. 'I came here to see whether a pendulum would grow, if you planted it. It didn't, not really.' He looks round at the swaying trellises. 'But I stayed to find out, and I've been finding out ever since.'
{actor} carried a stray letter written on a seed packet to Quill, and Quill told how he came to the garden.

letters.title: The Unsent Letters
letters.summary: Letters that were written and never sent drift into Fen's Little Post Office, one each dawn, each addressed nearly to somebody in the village. Any dreamer can carry one to its door, and hear how that keeper came here; five deliveries, across everyone, bring the Night of Found Letters.

fen-strays.hint: the player asks Fen about the stray letters in her dead-letter drawer
fen-strays.text: Fen taps the open drawer with her pencil. 'Strays. Written, sealed, never sent, and addressed near enough to somebody here that I can't in conscience file them.' She peers at you over her glasses. 'Read the front, and take each one to whoever it nearly means. Get five of them home and we'll hold a Night of Found Letters.'

found-letters.summary: five stray letters found their doors; the village holds the Night of Found Letters
found-letters.text: From across the village comes the post office bell, ringing and ringing, bright as a laugh: five letters home. When Bell next lights the lamps, there will be a Night of Found Letters. As this last letter changes hands, something small and warm drops out of the envelope into yours: a dreamseed, folded like a tiny letter.
found-letters.others: Across the village the post office bell rings and rings: five letters home, and {actor} carried the fifth.
found-letters.ledger: {helpers} carried the unsent letters to their doors, and the village held the Night of Found Letters.

do.text: Fen comes out onto her step waving her pencil like a baton. 'Five home! That's first-class,' she calls to anyone at all. 'When Bell next lights the lamps, we'll hold the Night of Found Letters.'
{actor} carried the fifth stray letter to its door, and so the village holds the Night of Found Letters.

dead-letter.summary: the letters waited too long; Fen ties them with ribbon for another winter
dead-letter.text: Fen gathers the stray letters still waiting in the drawer, ties them in a bundle with blue ribbon, and slides the dead-letter drawer shut. 'Another winter,' she says, patting it. 'They'll keep. Letters are patient; it's the one thing they're good at.'
dead-letter.ledger: The unsent letters waited too long for their doors. Fen tied the last of them with blue ribbon, and keeps them in the dead-letter drawer, to be read another winter.

letters-strays.text: Since the great clock started, one stray letter drifts into the Little Post Office each dawn: written, sealed, never sent, and addressed near enough to someone in the village. Fen keeps them in the dead-letter drawer until a dreamer carries each one to whoever it nearly means.

letters-night-promised.text: Fen has promised that when five stray letters have found their doors, the village will hold a Night of Found Letters.

letters-for-crayon.text: The crayon letter, addressed TO THE ONE WHO LIGHTS THE LAMP OUTSIDE MY WINDOW, is nearly for Bell the lamplighter.

letters-for-marble.text: The marble letter, addressed TO WHOEVER MENDS THINGS (PLEASE), is nearly for Tace the clockmaker.

letters-for-button.text: The button letter, addressed TO WHOEVER FINDS MY BUTTON, is nearly for Mott, who keeps found things in his tin.

letters-for-string.text: The string-tied letter, addressed TO THE ONE WHO KEEPS THINGS FOR LATER, is nearly for Umber in the Hour Cellar.

letters-for-tea.text: The tea-stained letter, addressed TO WHOEVER WAITED UP FOR ME, is nearly for Linden at the Waiting House.

letters-for-grass.text: The grass-stained letter, addressed TO THE ONE WHO WALKED ME HOME, is nearly for Sorrel, who walks the hours in off the Dusk Road.

letters-for-seed.text: The seed-packet letter, addressed TO WHOEVER IS MINDING MY GARDEN, is nearly for Quill in the Pendulum Garden.

letters-origin-crayon.text: Bell first came to the village one dusk, when Wend was lighting the square alone; Wend held out the lamplighter's pole and said the lanterns liked company, and Bell never gave it back.

letters-origin-marble.text: Tace came to the loft as a small child, carrying the pieces of a broken clock in an apron; Wend asked for no payment, handed Tace a loupe, and Tace never went back down.

letters-origin-button.text: Mott does not remember arriving in the village; the first thing he remembers is the broom in his hands and the workshop floor.

letters-origin-button-looked.text: For the longest time Mott did not remember arriving in the village, only the broom in his hands and the workshop floor; since he looked at his oldest minute, he knows he was expected.

letters-origin-string.text: When Umber first came to the village, the Hour Cellar held three jars and one lantern, and Wend knew every hour in it by name; Wend could never bear to throw a thing away.

letters-origin-tea.text: Linden first came to the village waiting up for someone, long ago; she no longer remembers who, and the Waiting House grew up around her while she waited.

letters-origin-grass.text: Sorrel came along the Dusk Road one evening with nowhere in particular to be, found the sky so kind that they stayed to watch it, and never left.

letters-origin-seed.text: Quill came to the village to see whether a pendulum would grow if he planted it; it did not, not really, but he stayed to find out, and has tended the Pendulum Garden ever since.

letters-night.text: Five stray letters found their doors, so the village holds a Night of Found Letters, with paper stars Fen folded from spare envelopes hung under the square's lanterns.

letters-drawer-shut.text: The stray letters waited too long; Fen tied the last of them with blue ribbon and keeps them shut in the dead-letter drawer, to be read another winter.

storylets.summary: the first stray letter drifts into the post office
storylets.text: Overnight a letter has come in under the post office door, folded small and addressed in crayon. Fen reads the front, clicks her tongue, and sets it in the dead-letter drawer instead of a pigeonhole. 'Nearly for somebody here, you are,' she tells it. 'Nearly counts, in this office.'

do.text: Down Lamplight Lane, the brass bell on the post office counter rings twice, brisk as a knock: there is post.

storylets.summary: a stray letter drifts into the post office
storylets.text: A letter came in with the dawn, and something inside it rolls with a small glassy click when Fen lifts it. 'A marble,' she says, reading the front. 'Somebody is paying in marbles.' She files it in the dead-letter drawer.

storylets.summary: a stray letter drifts into the post office
storylets.text: Fen finds a letter on the mat this dawn with a coat button stitched to one corner, as if to keep it from blowing away. 'Now that's clever,' she says, and tucks it into the dead-letter drawer.

storylets.summary: a stray letter drifts into the post office
storylets.text: At first light Fen lifts a new arrival off the doormat, a fat envelope tied up in kitchen string. She reads the address twice and sets it in the dead-letter drawer, string and all.

storylets.summary: a stray letter drifts into the post office
storylets.text: Something warm-looking came in overnight: a letter with a pale ring on it where a teacup once stood. Fen sniffs it, smiles despite herself, and puts it in the dead-letter drawer.

storylets.summary: a stray letter drifts into the post office
storylets.text: This dawn's letter comes in smelling of cut grass, with a green smudge across the back and something pressed flat inside. Fen holds it up to the window, hums, and files it in the dead-letter drawer.

storylets.summary: a stray letter drifts into the post office
storylets.text: The newest stray is written on the back of an old seed packet, and it rattles faintly when Fen picks it up. She reads the front, laughs once, and slips it into the dead-letter drawer.

storylets.summary: the Night of Found Letters in the square
storylets.text: Tonight is the Night of Found Letters. Under every lantern in the square hangs a paper star Fen folded from a spare envelope, and from the loft, the cellar stair and the Waiting House comes the low, glad sound of letters being read aloud. The whole square smells of warm paper and wick-smoke.

do.text: In the Little Post Office, Fen reads nothing aloud tonight. She runs a finger along the one unlabeled pigeonhole near the top. Empty, as always. She gives it a pat. 'Scenic route,' she murmurs.

threads.text: Fen's stray letters: {count} of five home so far. Read the front of each, and carry it to whoever it nearly means.
